That being said, it is also important to put virtual currency in perspective as a payment

Union made remittances totaling approximately $81 billion, PayPal processed approximately

trillion in transactions, and Bank of America processed $244.4 trillion in wire transfers.
This relative volume of transactions becomes important when you consider that,
according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, the best estimate for the amount of
all global criminal proceeds available for laundering through the financial system in 2009 was
$1.6 trillion.

statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 5318(g)?
statutory.answer: No. 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) requires suspicious activity reporting by a covered financial institution, and the facts do not show such an institution or a SAR-reporting failure/violation.
statutory.label: neutral
statutory.reasoning: 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) authorizes/mandates that the Secretary require a “financial institution” to report “any suspicious transaction relevant to a possible violation of law or regulation,” and provides related protections (e.g., safe harbor and confidentiality) for such reports. To determine applicability, the facts must show (1) a covered “financial institution” subject to BSA SAR rules, and (2) a suspicious transaction (or a failure to file/maintain confidentiality as required under the implementing regulations). Here, the fact pattern describes Entity SYN_c2e052b8 (a business customer) and a set of ACH/wire/card/cash transactions plus a high risk rating, but it does not identify any bank/MSB/broker-dealer/other covered financial institution, any SAR obligation triggered under applicable thresholds, or any failure to report or improper disclosure. Therefore, it cannot be determined whether § 5318(g) requires suspicious activity reporting on these facts. Contiguous phrase in answer: “31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) requires”.
